checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity (tb-016): compute_requests_hash MUST process each request exactly once. No request MUST be hashed twice.

audit_items.state_context: testing/middleware/builder/builder.go: retrievePendingBlockElectra() -> modifyExecutionPayload(result.Requests) -> executableDataToBlock() -> gethTypes.CalcRequestsHash(requests). File is in testing/middleware/ (test-only infrastructure, not production consensus code).

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: The executableDataToBlock function in the testing builder middleware invokes CalcRequestsHash on a requests [][]byte slice sourced directly from the EL response without any deduplication or ordering validation. The EL's ExecutionRequests array is copied byte-for-byte during JSON unmarshalling. No guard prevents duplicate entries from being hashed more than once.
state_anomalies_found: No deduplication of requests slice before passing to CalcRequestsHash
No ordering enforcement on requests before hashing
EL response is trusted unconditionally for request list contents
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching of requests between calls; each GetPayloadV4 response is processed independently. State inconsistency possible if duplicate entries are present.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: No concurrent access to the requests slice; the builder processes one payload at a time. Not a concurrency issue.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: A malicious or faulty EL returning duplicate entries in executionRequests would cause CalcRequestsHash to process each duplicate, producing a hash that differs from the hash of the canonical deduplicated list. This is constructable with a crafted JSON response at the engine API boundary.
phase2_symbolic_execution.counterexample: executionRequests: [0x01<deposit_data>, 0x01<deposit_data>] (same type byte 0x01, same payload, duplicated) causes CalcRequestsHash to hash 2 entries instead of 1, producing a wrong RequestsHash in the header.
attack_scenarios: Malicious EL sends duplicate execution requests; test middleware accepts and hashes them twice
Buggy EL implementation generates duplicate entries; test middleware does not filter them
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: None — this is a structural issue, not timing-dependent.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: The affected code is in testing/middleware/builder/builder.go, which is a test-only mock builder used in end-to-end test scenarios, not in production consensus logic. The production Prysm code path uses go-ethereum's own block assembly, not this middleware.
entry_points: engine_getPayloadV4 JSON-RPC response from mock EL in tests
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: Only reachable from test infrastructure. Not reachable from production P2P, RPC, or engine API in deployment.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The invariant 'each request hashed exactly once' is upheld by CalcRequestsHash itself (it processes each slice element once, sequentially). The vulnerability is that the slice may contain duplicates fed from the EL, which CalcRequestsHash cannot detect. In production, the EL is responsible for producing a canonical, deduplicated list; the CL trusts this. In this test middleware, the same trust model applies.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: CalcRequestsHash processes each element of the slice exactly once (single sequential loop in go-ethereum)
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient for the invariant as stated IF the input slice contains no duplicates. The guard does not enforce input uniqueness — that is the EL's responsibility per the Engine API spec.
edge_cases: EL sends duplicate request entries (protocol violation by EL, not a CL bug)
Empty requests slice (handled correctly: requestsHash remains nil)

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: Code is in testing/middleware/builder/ which is test infrastructure only. The production consensus path does not use this code. The property depends on EL correctness (protocol guarantee), not on Prysm's own deduplication. CalcRequestsHash correctly processes each provided element exactly once.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No fix required in production code. If desired for test correctness, add assertion in test middleware that no duplicate request type prefixes exist in the EL response.

EIP-7702 Authorization is an execution layer concept (transaction type in go-ethereum/EL clients). Prysm, as a CL client, treats EL transactions as opaque byte blobs and does not parse Authorization fields.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: N/A — no Authorization nonce handling in Prysm.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: No code path exists in Prysm to exploit. The EL is responsible for enforcing U64 nonce semantics for EIP-7702 Authorizations.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: Completely unreachable in Prysm. This is an EL-layer concern.

phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: N/A — property belongs to EL layer

checklist_item.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity (tb-020): In parse_deposit_requests, the address comparison log.address == DEPOSIT_CONTRACT_ADDRESS MUST be an exact byte comparison.

audit_items.state_context: Prysm does not implement parse_deposit_requests. Log address filtering (log.address == DEPOSIT_CONTRACT_ADDRESS) is done at the EL layer (go-ethereum) before DepositRequest objects are sent to Prysm via engine_getPayloadV4/engine_newPayloadV4. Prysm's DepositRequestsStarted function (process_block_helpers.go:520-535) is used to check the deposit mechanism migration state, not for address filtering.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: Prysm does not implement parse_deposit_requests log address filtering. This is delegated entirely to the execution layer (go-ethereum) per EIP-6110. Prysm receives pre-filtered DepositRequest objects via engine API and processes them without re-validating the source contract address. VerifyBlockDepositLength only checks deposit counts, not addresses.
state_anomalies_found: Prysm trusts EL to correctly filter deposit requests by contract address with no independent verification
No address re-validation in ProcessDepositRequests or processDepositRequest
phase1_abstract_interpretation.cache_analysis: No caching of deposit request source addresses. Each block's requests are processed fresh from EL.
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: No concurrent access issues in this path. Sequential processing per block.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: To exploit, an attacker must compromise the EL or exploit a bug in go-ethereum's parse_deposit_requests (not Prysm code). A malicious EL could inject deposit requests from wrong addresses, and Prysm would process them. This requires EL compromise, not a Prysm implementation flaw.
attack_scenarios: Compromised/malicious EL sends deposit requests from non-DEPOSIT_CONTRACT_ADDRESS; Prysm processes them without address validation — but this is an EL trust boundary issue, not a Prysm bug
go-ethereum bug in address comparison (e.g., case sensitivity) — would be a go-ethereum vulnerability, not Prysm

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: The parse_deposit_requests address comparison code does not exist in Prysm. It is implemented entirely in go-ethereum. The engine API boundary is the trust boundary. Prysm cannot be exploited for this property without first compromising go-ethereum.
entry_points: engine_newPayloadV4 from peer proposer via beacon P2P
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: EL (go-ethereum) is the implementation boundary for this property. Prysm has no code to exploit.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The EIP-6110 specification delegates deposit request parsing (including address filtering) to the EL. Prysm's implementation correctly follows this delegation. VerifyBlockDepositLength enforces count invariants per spec. The address comparison invariant is guaranteed by EL correctness, which is outside Prysm's scope.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: EL (go-ethereum) address filtering at parse_deposit_requests; Prysm's count check via VerifyBlockDepositLength
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient per EIP-6110 design — address filtering is the EL's responsibility
edge_cases: Malicious EL violating the protocol contract (outside Prysm's trust model)
go-ethereum address comparison bug (outside Prysm's codebase)

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: The parse_deposit_requests address comparison is an execution layer function not implemented in Prysm. Per EIP-6110, the EL is responsible for filtering deposit logs by contract address. Prysm correctly trusts the EL's output at the engine API boundary. No Prysm code implements or is required to implement log.address comparison.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: Audit go-ethereum's parse_deposit_requests implementation for address comparison correctness if desired.

checklist_item.title: Verify Invariant: The extract_deposit_data validation checks MUST be performed in the exact order ...

audit_items.state_context: DepositRequestFromConsensus is a stateless JSON conversion (no security validation). ToConsensus is called from REST API request parsing (external HTTP callers). All validations use DecodeHexWithLength (enforces exact byte length via two-step check: string pre-length then post-decode byte length) and ParseUint with bitSize=64 (enforces uint64 range). No shared mutable state. Sequential independent per-field validation with early return on error.

phase1_abstract_interpretation.summary: DepositRequestFromConsensus is a pure conversion function with no validation — it encodes already-validated consensus types to JSON strings. ToConsensus validates each field independently (pubkey, withdrawalCredentials, amount, signature, index) with DecodeHexWithLength or ParseUint, each enforcing exact sizes. The property's reference to 'exact order (1) data length (2) index size' does not map to a meaningful security dependency in this implementation.
state_anomalies_found: No security-relevant ordering dependency between data length checks and index size check in ToConsensus
DecodeHexWithLength has a two-step length check (pre-decode string length, post-decode byte length) — both are correct and complementary
ParseUint for index enforces uint64 range; overflow impossible
phase1_abstract_interpretation.concurrency_analysis: Stateless functions with no shared mutable state. No concurrency issues.

phase2_symbolic_execution.summary: All field validations in ToConsensus are independent with sequential early returns. No exploit scenario exists where the ordering of data length vs index size checks enables a bypass. Each check independently rejects invalid input. ParseUint(d.Index, 10, 64) cannot overflow as the 64-bit size constraint is enforced by the standard library.
attack_scenarios: Malformed hex pubkey: caught by DecodeHexWithLength before index check — no security impact from ordering
Index value exceeding uint64: caught by ParseUint with bitSize=64 — returns error
Empty index string: ParseUint returns error — no bypass possible
Odd-length hex string for pubkey: caught by hexutil.Decode — no bypass
phase2_symbolic_execution.timing_dependencies: None — synchronous validation, no state mutation on failure.

phase2_5_reachability_analysis.summary: ToConsensus is reachable via the REST API from external HTTP clients (validators, tooling). However, all validation paths return errors without state mutation, so reachability of this code does not enable exploitation. DepositRequestFromConsensus is a read-only conversion with no security impact.
entry_points: REST API request parsing (engine/beacon API consumers)
Internal beacon chain processing of execution requests
phase2_5_reachability_analysis.attack_surface: External HTTP API callers can supply arbitrary JSON DepositRequest objects; ToConsensus validates all fields independently. No bypass identified.

phase3_invariant_proving.summary: The validation ordering invariant from the property spec (data length before index size) has no security-relevant meaning in the Prysm implementation because the checks are independent. The implementation satisfies a stronger invariant: all fields are independently validated with no dependency on ordering. ParseUint with bitSize=64 prevents index overflow. DecodeHexWithLength with explicit length parameter prevents length mismatches.
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_identified: DecodeHexWithLength (enforces exact byte length for pubkey, withdrawalCredentials, signature); ParseUint(s, 10, 64) (enforces uint64 range for amount and index)
phase3_invariant_proving.guard_sufficiency: Sufficient — all fields validated independently, no ordering dependency creates a security gap. Both the string-length pre-check and post-decode byte-length check in DecodeHexWithLength are sound.
edge_cases: Odd-length hex string: caught by hexutil.Decode
Index = math.MaxUint64 + 1: caught by ParseUint bitSize=64 overflow detection
Empty pubkey string: DecodeHexWithLength fails at hexutil.Decode step
data length check and index check are independent — no interaction

phase3_5_scope_filtering.reason: No exploitable vulnerability exists. The validation order does not create a security dependency in this implementation. All field validations are independent, use appropriate type-safe library functions (DecodeHexWithLength, ParseUint with bitSize constraint), and return errors on any invalid input without mutating state. The property's ordering requirement is irrelevant to security here.
phase3_5_scope_filtering.recommendation: No fix required. The implementation correctly validates all fields independently with appropriate bounds checking.
